title: Smallpox: from variolation and Jenner's cowpox vaccine to eradication in 1980

sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.title: History of Smallpox
Meyer, Ehmann & Smith (2020), Smallpox in the Post-Eradication Era
Vaccine: From vacca, a cow
sources.note: 只取 vaccine 一詞源自拉丁文 vacca（牛）這一點

facts.text: Smallpox was caused by the variola virus and existed for at least 3,000 years, judging from marks on Egyptian mummies.
On average, about 3 out of every 10 people who got smallpox died of it.
Many survivors were left with scars, sometimes severe; some became blind.
Smallpox is the only human disease, and the only infectious disease, that has been eradicated; there has been no recorded case for almost 50 years.
Before vaccines, people in parts of Asia and Africa practised variolation: material from smallpox sores was put into healthy people, for example scratched into the arm.
Variolation usually gave a milder illness and far fewer deaths than catching smallpox naturally, but it used material from the real disease.
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had had cowpox seemed protected from smallpox.
Jenner took matter from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and inoculated an 8-year-old boy, James Phipps; when later exposed to smallpox, the boy stayed healthy.
The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow, because the first vaccine used cowpox.
By the middle of the 20th century vaccination had eliminated smallpox in western Europe, North America and Japan (North America 1952, Europe 1953), but it persisted elsewhere.
WHO began a global plan to eradicate smallpox in 1959; it struggled with a lack of funds, staff, national commitment and vaccine supply.
An intensified eradication programme began in 1967, helped by a better freeze-dried vaccine that did not need refrigeration and by the bifurcated (forked) needle.
In the intensified programme, health workers searched for new cases, isolated patients, and vaccinated and quarantined their close contacts.
Smallpox infected only humans, so there was no animal reservoir for the virus.
The virus did not cause hidden long-term infections, so people did not become long-term carriers.
Smallpox caused a distinctive rash, which made cases easy to identify and their contacts easy to find.
Smallpox was eliminated from South America in 1971, Asia in 1975 and Africa in 1977.
The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook in Somalia, in 1977; he recovered.
In 1978 Janet Parker, a medical photographer in Birmingham, England, died of smallpox after being infected near smallpox research laboratories.
Scientists from 19 countries certified eradication in December 1979, and the World Health Assembly declared the world free of smallpox on 8 May 1980.
